Page title: Field notes on continuity in a changing control plane
Readable page content (Markdown):
## Introduction

A changing control plane receives updates from independent workers. Some updates finish after their original page has disappeared; others arrive while a reader is moving between chapters. This article compares a software review with a laboratory note. The same short labels can mean different things in those two settings, so each account keeps its own definitions.

Our first review began with a simple inventory. A source paragraph had an identifier, its present text, and a position in the reading order. An outgoing request captured those values before waiting for a response. The inventory deliberately excluded forms, drafts, navigation, hidden panels, and executable examples, because they were outside the authorized reading material.

We also separated the lifetime of a request from the lifetime of the article. A request could finish successfully but still belong to an old article. A reader could keep the same address open while an editor replaced the body. The address alone therefore did not prove that an earlier result still described the current material. A source comparison was required before a response could be attached.

An early prototype kept every paragraph in its reference message. It worked for a short note but became expensive for a manual. Sending the entire manual with each paragraph repeated information that the model had already seen and delayed the first useful result. The revised prototype kept only a small amount of evidence relevant to the current passage, with an explicit ceiling on characters and stored records.

The evaluation distinguishes transport correctness from language quality. A fixed response can show that the right source reached a service and that a canceled response was not published. It cannot establish whether a language model chose the right noun, resolved a reference, or respected a change of subject. For those questions we keep the original sentence beside the actual returned translation and record uncertain c

We also separated the lifetime of a request from the lifetime of the article. A request could finish successfully but still belong to an old article. A reader could keep the same address open while an editor replaced the body. The address alone therefore did not prove that an earlier result still described the current material.
